title: Eastern Europe
wiki_lead:
Eastern Europe is a subregion of the European continent. As a largely ambiguous term, it has a wide range of geopolitical, geographical, ethnic, cultural and socio-economic connotations. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, while its western boundary is defined in many different ways and has shifted over time. Narrow definitions, in which Central and Southeast Europe are counted as separate regions, include Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Broader definitions also include Moldova and Romania and some or all of the Balkans, though generally not Greece or East Thrace, and sometimes the Baltic states, the Visegrád Group countries and the Caucasus. Russia, by far the largest country in the world, is also the largest in the region.
The main socio-cultural characteristics of Eastern Europe have historically been defined largely by the traditions of the Slavs and by the influence of Eastern Christianity as it developed through the Eastern Roman Empire. The Cold War created another definition, in which "Eastern Europe" meant the communist states of the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc, separated from the West by the Iron Curtain.
The term is sometimes considered pejorative, through stereotypes of Eastern Europe as poorer and less developed than Western Europe, and the term Central and Eastern Europe is sometimes used as a more neutral grouping.
The region's history was shaped by the migrations of the Slavs in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Christianization of its peoples from both Rome and Constantinople, the Mongol invasions, and the rule of the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. After the First World War a series of new or restored states emerged, most of which were overrun by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union during the Second World War, when much of the region became a battlefield and the main site of the Holocaust. From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and after the Revolutions of 1989 many of its countries joined NATO and the European Union.
Much of the region lies on the East European Plain, which is drained by long rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, the Dnieper and the Danube, and its climate becomes more continental towards the east. Most of its states are parliamentary or semi-presidential republics, and eleven of them belong to the European Union, while Russia and Belarus give their presidents wide powers and were classed by Freedom House as consolidated authoritarian regimes. Since joining the EU several countries have moved closer to its average income per person, while Russia's economy relies heavily on the export of fossil fuels. Large-scale emigration and low fertility have reduced the population of many countries since 1990. The region's cultural traditions include Orthodox icon painting, the literature of writers such as Alexander Pushkin and Adam Mickiewicz, the music of Frédéric Chopin and scientific work such as Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table.

Definitions

Several definitions of Eastern Europe exist in the early 21st century, but they often lack precision and may be anachronistic. The term has been called "fuzzy", an idea that is continually being redefined. The historian Larry Wolff has argued that the idea of "Eastern Europe" was created in the 18th century by thinkers of the Enlightenment, who cultivated an image of its backwardness, and the literary scholar Thomas Grob traces it primarily to the French Enlightenment. In a paper for the United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names, the geographer Peter Jordan wrote that "every assessment of spatial identities is essentially a social and cultural construct".

grok_lead: Eastern Europe constitutes a subregion of the European continent, delineated by the United Nations geoscheme as comprising Belarus, Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Poland, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, the Russian Federation, Slovakia, and Ukraine. This area spans diverse geographical features, including the vast Eastern European Plain, the Carpathian Mountains, and coastlines along the Baltic, Black, and Caspian Seas, fostering a range of climates from temperate to continental. Historically, the region has been shaped by successive imperial dominions, including the Russian Empire, Austro-Hungarian Empire, and Ottoman Empire, culminating in post-World War II subjugation under Soviet control, where communist governments imposed centralized planning and suppressed political dissent across the Eastern Bloc. The Iron Curtain demarcation isolated these states from Western Europe, enforcing ideological conformity until the revolutions of 1989 triggered the collapse of communist regimes and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. In the contemporary era, Eastern European nations exhibit marked variation in political trajectories and economic performance, with severalâsuch as Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia, Romania, and Bulgaria âintegrating into the European Union and NATO, driving market-oriented reforms that yielded substantial GDP growth in outperformers like Poland, while others grapple with authoritarian consolidation in Belarus and ongoing conflict with Russian forces in Ukraine. Culturally, the region is characterized by Slavic linguistic dominance, a blend of Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic traditions, and resilient national identities forged through centuries of external pressures, contributing to both internal ethnic tensions and a collective emphasis on sovereignty amid geopolitical strains.
